learning: Expect to learn whether the wider, forward array reduces off-track exits at the same controller gain. If the robot still leaves early with max_error near 0.06 m, the controller gain or the signal scale is the next suspect; if it completes, speed becomes the next limit.
notes: Builder's iteration 1 geometry kept unchanged; controller re-tuned for the narrower track and wider array. Lower kp and higher kd than iteration 0, with base_speed reduced to 1.2, because iteration 0 failed by drifting off the line, not by running out of time.
rationale: Iteration 0 raced all 60 trials across oval, s-bend and slalom and every run went off track (finish rate 0). Progress stalled at 0.075 to 0.15, which is far short of the course, so runs ended well before the 3 s limit and speed was not the limiting factor. max_error (0.060 to 0.069 m) sat at or above the 0.06 m off-track floor, and line-loss events were 1 to 2 per run, so the robot was losing the line early and then drifting past the edge. steering_oscillation was modest (0.13 to 0.17), which argues against a gain that is too high causing chatter, and it argues for a controller that corrects drift sooner rather than one that oscillates. Because the Builder's geometry (wider array at y = 0.06, wheel_track 0.11, mass 0.7) is the thing under test, I keep it exactly as supplied. The narrower wheel_track raises the turn rate per unit of PWM difference by about 9 percent versus iteration 0, so I scale the proportional gain down slightly rather than raising it: kp goes from 3.0 to 2.5 to avoid overshoot on the bends the wider array will now see earlier. I add kd 0.3 (up from 0.1) to damp the faster-responding signal, and keep ki at 0 since no windup evidence exists. I lower base_speed from 1.4 to 1.2 because the runs failed by drifting off, not by running out of time; a slower robot gives the steering more time per bend. The time budget is then a question for a later iteration, once a run completes. line_loss stays 'last_direction', which is consistent with the robot losing the line on one side. Expected result: fewer off-track exits and max_error below about 0.05 m, with the robot still finishing some runs; if it does not finish any, the next step is speed, not gain. Telemetry requests add completion_time and noise_robustness so the time limit and disturbance sensitivity can be read directly.
